meta.title: Why MAU grew 20% but revenue stayed flat
meta.question: Monthly active users increased about 20% quarter over quarter, but revenue stayed nearly flat. What explains the difference?
meta.mode: Independent run · v2, corrected after peer review
meta.author: Product Analytics Agent (Claude Code)

items: Check N = one logged database query. Every number points to the check that produced it. The appendix lists all 21 checks in plain words.
Data layers: Gold = pre-built monthly tables, Silver = cleaned user-level tables, Bronze = raw records.
Signup groups: Q2 signups joined in April–June; Q3 signups joined in July–September. 30-day results leave out September signups, because their 30 days run past the end of the data (30 September).
Patterns, not proof: where the report says a pattern “suggests” something, the cause has not been proven.
MAU
Monthly active users: distinct signed-in people with at least one session in the month. The quarter figure is the average of its three months.
Net revenue
Successful charges minus refunds, counted on the day the payment succeeds. App-store fees and tax are not deducted.
Signup cohort
Everyone who created an account in the same calendar month. Example: the July cohort = all accounts created 1–31 July. We follow each cohort for its first 30 days.
Paywall
The screen that asks a user to subscribe or buy before watching premium content.
Paywall reach
Share of a signup cohort who saw at least one paywall within 30 days of their own signup time.
Paid within 30 days
Share of a signup cohort with a successful payment within 30 days of signing up (30-day paid conversion).
Unidentified session
A session we can't link to a signed-in user, so it isn't counted in MAU.
ARPU / ARPPU
Average revenue per active user / per paying user.

blocks.text: Recent signup cohorts show much lower recorded paywall reach and paid conversion. This suggests a problem early in the path to paying, but the data doesn't show whether the cause is user behaviour, product design, tracking or something else.

items: Who the new users are: all of the net MAU growth came from Q3 signups (+3,457 a month on average), mostly from paid social ads. Users who joined earlier fell by 1,654 (checks 6, 12).

What is different for them: they watch about as much as earlier signups (about 3.6 views in the first 30 days), but fewer saw a paywall (1.0% in July, 0.5% in August, versus 4.4% in May and 2.7% in June). Fewer paid within 30 days: 0.5% of July–August signups versus 1.9% of May–June signups (checks 7, 17).
Why revenue is flat: revenue = paying users × revenue per paying user, and both stayed flat (about 1,036 payers paying about $9.70 each) (checks 1, 5).

blocks.title: Not yet known:
blocks.text: why paywall reach and conversion fell, and whether showing more paywalls would raise conversion. Two data questions are also open: how many people sit behind unidentified sessions, and why checkouts from Q2 signups stopped reaching payment in August–September (chapter 05).

steps.goal: Where did the extra users come from, and did anything change on the money side? Gold tables answer this directly.

checks.name: H1 Growth comes from new users who don't pay
checks.result: Growth is in new users, mostly paid social; subscribers flat near 1,000.

checks.name: H2 Price, mix, refunds or failed payments offset growth
checks.result: Price $9.99 throughout; refunds under $40 a quarter; failure rate 5–6% in both quarters.

checks.name: H3 Growth limited to one platform or country
checks.result: Growth on every platform and in every country.

steps.next: Growth is new users who don't pay, so test why new users don't convert.

steps.goal: Why don't new users convert? Gold has cohort totals; splitting by source needs Silver.

checks.name: H4 Only paid social users convert worse
checks.result: Conversion fell to about 0.5% in every source, organic included.

checks.name: H5 Paywall views didn't grow with MAU
checks.result: About 1,000–1,050 paywall viewers a month from May on, while MAU grew.

checks.name: H6 New users rarely reach the paywall
checks.result: Pattern confirmed. Whether it causes lower conversion is not tested.

steps.next: Rule out content changes and measurement problems before trusting the pattern.

steps.goal: Could content or measurement explain the pattern? History and raw events need Bronze.

checks.name: H8 Unidentified sessions distort MAU
checks.result: Share is 6.5–7.6% and varies; how many people they represent is unknown.

checks.name: H9 Paywall events stopped being tracked
checks.result: Payments fall with paywall views, but that can't prove paywall events are complete.

steps.next: Budget of 3 rounds used. Pattern measured, cause not proven: report it and recommend a test and a tracking audit.

blocks.title: How the total change adds up
lines: The three groups don't overlap, so their changes add up to the total change in MAU:
9,016 (Q2 MAU) − 1,338 (signed up before April) − 316 (signed up in Q2) + 3,457 (signed up in Q3) = 10,819 (Q3 MAU)
Q3 signups had no activity in Q2 because they didn't exist yet, so their whole Q3 average counts as growth.

items: By acquisition source (check 6): paid social +1,841, paid search +92, unknown +25, organic −156. Paid social was 24% of May signups and 64% of July–August signups.
Revenue side (check 5): 99% of revenue is the $9.99 monthly subscription. About 1,000 subscribers pay each month; roughly 10% cancel each month and about as many join, so the base stays flat.

blocks.title: The maths behind the bars
lines: Saw a paywall % = signups who saw at least one paywall within 30 days ÷ all signups that month. Example: April 156 ÷ 1,600 = 9.8%.
Paid % = signups with a successful payment within 30 days ÷ all signups that month. Example: July 13 ÷ 2,477 = 0.5%.

Comparison used: May–June 94 ÷ 4,854 = 1.9% versus July–August 29 ÷ 5,426 = 0.5%. April is left out because the data starts with no subscribers; September is left out because its 30 days end after the data does.
Every 30-day payer also saw a paywall (check 17). That shows the two go together, not that the paywall causes payment.

blocks.text: All 9 explanations tested (the investigation path is in chapter 02):

rows: Growth comes from new users who don't pay
Paid social users +1,841 of the +1,803 total; subscribers flat near 1,000 (checks 4, 6, 12)
Price, product mix, refunds or failed payments offset growth
$9.99 price; refunds under $40 a quarter; failure rate 5–6% in both quarters (check 5)
Growth is limited to one platform or country
Growth on every platform and in every country (check 6)
Only paid social users convert worse
About 0.5% in every source for July–August signups (check 8)
Paywall views didn't grow with MAU
About 1,000–1,050 viewers a month from May; share of MAU 11.6% → 9.2% (check 9)
New users rarely reach the paywall
Reach 4.4% (May) → 0.5% (Aug) with similar viewing. Causal effect on conversion not tested (checks 14, 17)
6.5–7.6% of sessions, varying by month; the number of people they represent is unknown (check 15)
Doesn't rule out missing paywall events; needs an instrumentation audit (checks 16, 21)

blocks.title: Scenario, not a forecast:
blocks.text: if July–August signups (5,426) had paid at the May–June rate (1.9%), about 105 would have paid instead of 29. That is about 76 more subscribers × $9.99 ≈ $760 a month, around 7.6% of Q3's average monthly net revenue ($10,056). It assumes the rate is reachable, the price stays at $9.99 and these subscribers renew.
These issues don't invalidate the calculations on the current data snapshot. But their effect on how the history is read, and on the size of the movement, is not fully measured.

items: The data shows where new users stop, not why. Product release and campaign data aren't available.
PocketToons is synthetic data. Patterns here are associations, not proven causes.
First-30-day viewing figures use whole UTC days, so the first and last day are approximate. Paywall and payment figures use exact times.
Not checked: marketing spend vs new payers, which titles lead to paywalls, and subscriber churn by signup month.

Find what changed for new users around 1 July. Check onboarding, paywall placement and the paid social landing experience. Success check: 30-day paywall reach returns towards the May–June level (2.7–4.4%).
Audit paywall and checkout tracking. Confirm paywall events are complete, and explain why Q2 signups' checkouts stopped reaching payment in August–September. This decides whether H9 can be closed.
Track two early-warning metrics next to MAU: new-user paywall reach within 30 days, and 30-day paid conversion by source.
Judge paid social on payers, not active users. July–August paid social signups produced 18 payers. Compare spend with new payers before increasing the budget.
Test the cause with an A/B experiment: show a paywall prompt to new free users (for example, at the free-episode limit) to learn whether more exposure actually raises conversion.
